items.body:
Lil Cherry & GOLDBUUDA are bringing 'Yummy 88' to Singapore for its first-ever live performance.

The Korean-American hip-hop sibling duo will take the stage at The Vibe Tribe on 12 September, happening at Bae’s Cocktail Club in Chinatown. The late-night event will run from 11 PM to 4 AM, with the pair previewing their upcoming single ahead of its official release on 23 September.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bae’s (@baescocktailclub.sg)

Described as a mukbang anthem for food lovers, 'Yummy 88' celebrates food, indulgence, and good vibes. The single follows Lil Cherry & GOLDBUUDA’s viral 2020 track 'MUKKBANG!'.

Known for blending hip-hop, alternative pop, K-pop, electronic textures, and underground aesthetics, the duo have built a distinct identity through their experimental sound, visual style, and approach to storytelling.

Their Singapore appearance will be part of The Vibe Tribe, a recurring late-night event featuring high-energy DJ sets and guest performances. The night will also double as a birthday celebration for Singaporean hip-hop artist Shigga Shay.

items.body: Drone has an incredible tonal range. With sounds that range from calm to abrasive, drone can soothe or unsettle, like the distance between a refrigerator hum and an attack copter. These albums not only reflect the sounds that flow through our bodies, perceptible or not, but the hum, buzz and noise of everyday life. Earth’s empty aural spaces are being filled in slowly by sound, from subsonic frequency to passing plane. Those who work in this field underline the musical aspects of drone: subtle shifts, undulations, tension and release. Turning the intrusive into the sonically desired is yet another form of reclamation. Our cover image is from Marta Salogni & Stefano Pilia‘s Phren on Maple Death, covered below. As always, our discussion of drone begins with the amazing Room40 label, whose roster focuses on drone yet is in no way restricted to it. We’ll be listing all of the imprint’s fall announcements here, including those of Someone Good, since Lawrence English has done such a fine job with advance publicity and it looks tidy! The first is a re-release of David Shea‘s I, originally on Sub Rosa; the Zorn-influenced album still sounds fresh and raucous (September 2). Next on the schedule is Werner Defeldecker + Eliad Wagner‘s Fray Field; readers may recall Dafeldecker’s Fathom Tidea with Lawrence English from earlier this year. This improvised album of double bass, synth and guitar is a whole different beast (September 11). Jannis Anastasakis and Peter Knight follow with Feather, a two-and-a-half-hour performance distilled to 32 minutes, light as air (September 18). The month ends with Hannes Strobl‘s Resonance IBK, an immersive five-part piece that blends field recordings of mountain and valley with complementary, drone-like music, and Prime Frequencies from mHz, who brought us 2024’s Material Prosody. The latter album, available in code and web-based formats, contains 47 investigations of sine waves and their relationship to prime numbers (September 25).   Room40’s October slate begins with Andrew Tuttle & Darren Cross‘ AT/DC (no, that’s not a typo)! This warm guitar and banjo set is enhanced by reverb and synthesizer, reminiscent of Rain Drinkers (October 2). Winter comes early with Philip Samartzis & Michael Vorfeld‘s Atmospheric Pressure, an acoustic reflection of a 36-hour Antarctic blizzard (October 9). Matt Rösner‘s Lost Meridians follows, described as “music to pause to,” reflecting the peace of open prairies and wide, unpolluted skies (October 16). Yann Novak‘s Discontinuity is a remixed response to Continuity, as well as a commentary on “deteriorating conditions in the U.S.” (October 16). Bruno Duplant investigates the nature of erosion through sound, offering l’usure du socle stable du monde, a two-part study meant to be experienced as a single piece (October 23). Steven Hess + Rutger Zuydervelt follow Re:collecting exactly a decade later with Re:construct. Times have changed, but there’s always a place for hope (October 30).   Maple Death continues its fabulous run with another box set produced in conjunction with Opale. Phren is a collaborative effort from Marta Salogni & Stefano Pilia, introduced with an eleven-minute hymn that turns out to be the album’s most sedate selection, a worthy closer after the weight of the preceding tracks. The cover art is only the beginning; more of Sarah Mazzetti’s illustrations lie within (October 2). zakè‘s Tide Requiem for the Low Sea is a beauty to behold, available on increasingly rare picture disc vinyl. The music is like the end of summer, the art like an invitation to extend the season (September 2). The Sirens begins with the sound of an observatory door being opened. Geologist & Kyle Simon‘s music twinkles and shines, like a planetarium score or the biography of starlight (Outside Time, October 16). Calum Builder plays a reconstructed Copenhagen pipe organ on Although Changed, I Arise the Same, accompanied by vocal fragments culled from the Psalms. This results is a double reconstruction of faith and sound (thanatosis, September 25).   Tehran-born, Berlin-based Ava Rasti‘s No One Knows How Wild the Wind Blows is a harrowing reflection on current conditions in Iran. Aslan Mohammadpour‘s video for the title track starts as a benign home video before literally pulling back the curtain (FatCat / 130701, October 30). Falling into dark ambient-drone territory with titles such as “Circle of Black Candles,” Ajna‘s Mysterium Tremendum can’t wait for sunset. On this album, darkness is meant to evoke transcendence as well as fear (Winter-Light, September 4). Eric Angelo Bessel‘s Illusion of an Inland Ocean is murky, dark and mysterious, a reflection of everything from the ocean depths to the depths of the soul (Lore City Music, October 30). Seven bagpipe players and three basin players create an enveloping sound on Erwan Keravec‘s There will be no miracles here; check this video for insight on the performance. The organic sound borders on the otherworldly (Buda Musique, October 16). Rachel Shearer honors the earth and the Māori concept of whakapapa on Te Oro o Te Ao, as Maori vocals give way to a massive wall of field recordings and lead to a peaceful denouement (Thin Wrist Recordings, October 9). Falsetto singing, harmonium and cassette are the hallmarks of KKKAAARRREEENNNIIINNNAAA, an album as wild as its spelling bee title, courtesy of Charlemagne Palestine / Oren Ambarchi / Daniel O’Sullivan (Black Truffle, September 10).   Kai Niggemann‘s Climate and Violence began as music for the theatre performance “Denkraum der Utopien,” and has been updated and tweaked for this release. Since then, global climate change has only accelerated, and threatens to increase exponentially. The morphing music reflects shifts in atmospheric conditions and long-range forecasts (WAF80 Music, September 25). Giulio Aldinucci‘s Materia treats sound as matter that can be sculpted; the pieces feel like clay, molded and remolded, resisting their final forms (Karlrecords, September 18). Haarvöl‘s Overflowed Shelters is a direct commentary on recent events, highlighted by the harrowing first single, “Perpetual Ruins (a lament for Gaza).” The music reflects a slow-motion genocide, a horror from which many turn away, but that demands to be seen and confronted. There’s no escape in this music, nor should there be (Moving Furniture, September 26).   Thomas Brinkmann‘s GETGETGET is a single piece in two parts, born of a live performance. Listening is like traveling through the various permutations of drone, thin to thick, soft to loud, with percussion serving as additional texture (Editions Mego, October 23). A “diverse ecology of machines” is used on Ben Carey‘s INVENTIONS, which at times sounds like a cathedral tower and at other times a factory floor (Hospital Hill, September 14). Markus Solid creates immersive atmospheres by combining drone and electronics. Elastic Embrace is as mutable as its title, bent forward and back, refusing to break (Rhizome, September 25). ARROWOUNDS‘ Fludiic Time Cathedral is dark and mysterious, as one might expect from the artist who brought us In the Octopus Pond. The style is gothic rock drenched in shoegaze timbres, removed from the ether while still dripping, a worthy finale for Lost Tribe Sound’s Moss & Melee series (September 25). Richard Allen

items.body: For fans of CPU, Carl Finlow and electro’s wider continuum, IXRQ‘s command of the language will be immediately apparent. But this isn’t simply reverence for what has been. These are familiar components arranged with enough curiosity to remind us that electro’s future has never been about inventing the machine. It’s about continuing to find new things for it to say. Robotronic instruction sit beneath the surface Form & Fashion by IXRQ   A year after The Future Is Plastic, IXRQ returns to a form that has always understood the future as something assembled from memory. Electro is, after all, a genre built on recurring signals: machines imagining themselves as human, humans imagining themselves as machines, and a handful of sounds carrying decades of accumulated meaning. Across these four cuts, IXRQ works fluently within that vocabulary while resisting the temptation to simply reproduce it. The European lens is unmistakable. Rotherian propulsion and robotronic instruction sit beneath the surface, but the EP’s pleasures are found in its details: 808 patterns that groove rather than merely function, clipped Ensoniq fragments, synth probes disappearing into reverb, and pads that open up spaces where the rhythm can momentarily lose its certainty. Vocoders issue commands, naturally, but there is something pleasingly ambiguous about who exactly is listening. Creating tension between the archetypal and th​e individual :: That tension between the archetypal and th​e individual gives the EP its shape. “I Am Modeled” arrives with stoic authority, its clipped commands establishing an atmosphere of cool, programmed detachment, while “Signal Bridge” tightens the machinery into taut, economical funk, finding its momentum in crisp interplay between rhythm and circuitry. Personal favorite “Opal Tilt” pushes the established syntax further, its fat bass and subtly displaced ideas suggesting a system beginning to think beyond its programming, bending the familiar grammar into something altogether more playful and physical. Closer “XPVC Cascer,” meanwhile, alters the equation through pace alone, accelerating the final transmission into a more urgent, restless space. For fans of CPU, Carl Finlow and electro’s wider continuum, IXRQ‘s command of the language will be immediately apparent. But this isn’t simply reverence for what has been. These are familiar components arranged with enough curiosity to remind us that electro’s future has never been about inventing the machine. It’s about continuing to find new things for it to say. Form & Fashion is available on SEQ:RUN. [Bandcamp] Form & Fashion by IXRQThe post IXRQ :: Form & Fashion EP (SEQ:RUN) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Concept Record not only works as a creative tool; it demonstrates what can be created when Professor Ben’s instruction is heeded. The concept is to use this record alongside other records to make new records, while providing a legitimate D.H.S. album of its own right—one that embraces the features that help make physical records so fun and appealing. The record is the concept Concept Record by Dimensional Holofonic Sound   Ben Stokes is no stranger to concept albums. The albums he has released this century as Dimensional Holofonic Sound (D.H.S., to the initiated) and under the moniker Quietworld could all legitimately be labeled “concept records.” 2002’s Attention Earth People was an ode to ’50s and ’60s sci-fi and outer space. The “disturbing Muzak” of Quietworld’s Relaxalot was like walking through a Backrooms-style retro shopping mall—a boomer’s advertising fever dream. Then came D.H.S.’s 2020 music visualizer, Seeing Is Believing, with the vinyl edition even including a pair of classic red-and-blue glasses for watching the album’s videos online in 3D. Oh, let’s not forget his hand in the Tino’s Breaks series, led by an action figure who serves as an instructor in Latin beats. So it may seem a bit on the nose that D.H.S.’s new album is titled Concept Record—until you spend time with what Stokes has crafted here. After a couple of playthroughs, you realize the title could also be presented as “Concept: Record,” because on this album, the record is the concept. Fully realized jams :: Concept Record is a self-proclaimed “instrument disguised as an album,” according to Dimensional Holofonic Sound’s Bandcamp page, where you can currently pick up both digital and vinyl versions if you’re attentive and lucky enough. That description is certainly apt. Many of the tracks are ripe for a DJ’s arsenal, with loads of potential—and actual—loops throughout. Turntable DJs and creators are especially well equipped, as the double-vinyl version contains fifteen locked grooves with eternally repeating loops that stop only when you lift the needle. This isn’t merely a scratching record or DJ tool, though. While there are dedicated loop tracks and spoken vignettes, the majority of the album consists of fully realized jams. Many tracks begin stripped back or include sparser sections, seemingly designed to be sampled and looped into new creations, but D.H.S. expertly layers bouncing bass, bleeping synths, effects, and samples onto his beats, building them into genuinely danceable ravers. Stokes pulls out all his best tricks for this offering, treating us to a smorgasbord of what he’s learned over the last three decades. His ability to evoke nostalgic futurism through vintage dialogue and samples paired with modern electronic sounds is evident from the get-go in the arpeggiated title track, “Concept Record.” There’s the Quietworld-tinged “Hospital Tent,” the glitchy unease of “Chatter,” and the dark horror of “Chit Chat.” His prowess with cut-and-paste breakbeat rhythms is on full display in the Tino-esque “Maestro Music” and caffeinated “Takeoffthecoffeepotweputitdownupright,” and there’s bleep bliss found in the lead single “Supersonic Holofonic,” and cuts “Electro Pop” and “Concept Music,” the latter featuring Oakland musician Konceptualizer. Is that meta enough for you? Concept Record is another winning concept :: What shines brightest—and will have you throwing a personal mini-rave in your living room—is the acid, and D.H.S. serves up a potent dose. “Green Acid (Jack Dangers Remix)” is a clear standout, and having Dangers drop in is yet another brilliant treat from Stokes’ bag of tricks. The aforementioned “Supersonic Holofonic” is burbly enough to keep the trip going, blending into the electro-acid of “Cut To Black,” followed by the flashback of the buoyant “Full Blackout.” Now where did I put those glow sticks? In the end, Concept Record is another winning concept from Ben Stokes. He gives us the record as a musical tool, embodied in the vinyl’s locked-groove loops, and the record as a cohesive collection of songs. The LPs also serve as a unique listening experience, with a slightly altered track order, extra bits, and alternate versions/edits. (“Cut To Black” has a completely different vibe and mix on the vinyl.) Sides 1 and 3 even have zoetrope labels. You can only get that on a record. An electrified voice at the beginning of “Electro Pop”—at least on the digital version—sums up a core idea well, commanding the listener to “Do things… don’t fritter away your time… create, act… and be somebody.” Concept Record not only works as a creative tool; it demonstrates what can be created when Professor Ben’s instruction is heeded. The concept is to use this record alongside other records to make new records, while providing a legitimate D.H.S. album of its own right—one that embraces the features that help make physical records so fun and appealing. Concept Record succeeds on all counts. A+. Concept Record is available on Bandcamp. Concept Record by Dimensional Holofonic Sound  The post Dimensional Holofonic Sound :: Concept Record (Self Released) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: There’s something particularly satisfying about hearing forgotten tracks recovered, revisited and finally released for others to discover. Off-Cuts (2014–2021) doesn’t feel like a scattered collection of archival material; instead, it comes across as a carefully gathered snapshot of a creative period, proving that these pieces still have plenty to say. Serving as a fine snapshot of the artist’s creative phase Off-Cuts (2014–2021) by Scarper   Steve Young (aka Scarper) continues to navigate a world of abstract electronics, consistently catching our attention through his output on his own Plexus imprint. Aptly titled Off-Cuts (2014–2021), this release brings together previously unreleased tracks from his Warmer Squares and E-Funk periods—pieces that might otherwise have remained buried within Young’s personal catalog, now recovered and given a new life. Serving as a fine snapshot of the artist’s creative phase across these seven years, all eight tracks have aged remarkably well, revealing qualities that feel less like forgotten leftovers and more like sounds waiting to be rediscovered. “Synet (Dial-Upp ’00 Mix)” immediately transports us back to the modem-era haze of the ’90s, cascading into an ambient swirl of sonic activity, soundtrack-like fragments and imploding, beat-driven beauty. “Rinse & Repeat (Head & Shoulders Mix)” ventures further into ambient techno territory, while the more upfront “Nightshift (Acid Tuesday Mix)” shuffles bass and percussion into a frenetic, dancefloor-ready rush. It’s within the (somewhat) slower pieces, though​, that Young really opens things up. The erratic, glitch-infested pulse of “Outlier (You’re My Skweeero Mix)” feels congested and fractured as it moves through downtempo breakbeat strains, while standout “Polarity (Curse These Metal Hands Mix)” dips into acidic waters with a full-throttle techno drive, its abstract substructures constantly shifting beneath the surface. Toward the tail end, the release takes a distinctive electro-infused turn. “Ponderosa (Grilled T-Bone Mix)” pushes Young’s sound into more elevated territory, while the crunchy drum’n’bass collision of “Steppe (Runty-Bunting Mix)” feels remarkably fresh, regardless of when it was originally created. Bringing things to a chilled-out close, “Halocline (Deep Water Mix)” bubbles to the surface through finely shaped micro-melodies and a deeply nostalgic flutter that feels capable of drifting on indefinitely. There’s something particularly satisfying about hearing forgotten tracks recovered, revisited and finally released for others to discover. Off-Cuts (2014–2021) doesn’t feel like a scattered collection of archival material; instead, it comes across as a carefully gathered snapshot of a creative period, proving that these pieces still have plenty to say. Off-Cuts (2014 – 2021) is available on Plexus. [Bandcamp] Off-Cuts (2014–2021) by ScarperThe post Scarper :: Off-Cuts (2014 – 2021) (Plexus) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Lee “Scratch” Perry recorded his vocal for “Angels” at Black Ark Studio in Switzerland over a decade before the song reached its final form, laying it over a rough beat with the words: “When I recorded the vocals, I only listened to the heartbeat.” Born Rainford Hugh Perry in Jamaica, Perry spent the 1960s and 70s building the foundations of dub from his Black Ark Studio in Kingston, producing Bob Marley and the Wailers, Junior Murvin and the Congos before relocating first to London and then to Switzerland. Steve Marshall, the English producer who returned to the unfinished rhythm years later, added new drums, electric guitar, piano and synth, steering the track toward Lovers Rock. Geo Baddoo, the Somerset-raised, London-based soul and R&B artist, joined the project after that, writing a gentle, contemplative lyric that pushed “Angels” further into Lovers Rock territory. Baddoo built her opening lines around a refrain Perry had left in the vocal, drawn from Psalm 87:7: “singers and players of the instruments.” Dennis Bovell, the Barbados-born producer credited with shaping UK Lovers Rock in the 1970s, handled the single’s dub mix. “Angels” leads Scratch Is Alive, due on State of Emergency on 13 November and timed to mark what would have been Perry’s 90th birthday in 2026. It’s the fifth album Perry and Marshall have made together, following the Grammy-nominated The End Of An American Dream and Revelation, and it gathers unreleased vocal and dub recordings made in Switzerland and London. Stream “Angels” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Lee “Scratch” Perry x Geo Baddoo – Angels appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by Abrasmatheus — This was my first time listening to No Earthly Connection, and I came to it with high expectations. I have always been a big fan of Yes, so I already knew how impressive Rick Wakeman could be with keyboards. Even so, this album was a very pleasant surprise.From the beginning, I was impressed by the beautiful melodies and the strongly progressive character of the music. I would describe it mainly as Symphonic Prog, Progressive Rock and, of course, with strong Classical influences. The arrangements are complex, grandiose, melodic and atmospheric, but the music never loses its emotional side.Rick Wakeman is obviously the great highlight here. This album is a wonderful showcase of his talent with keyboards and synthesizers. Many of the things I love about his playing in Yes are present here as well, but in a more personal setting where he can really show what he is capable of. His synthesizers give the album an enormous sense of grandeur.I also really enjoyed the way the album works as a complete experience. I always appreciate progressive rock albums that encourage you to sit down and listen to the whole record instead of simply picking individual songs. No Earthly Connection works particularly well in this format.The concept is another aspect that made the album special to me. The first five sections form Music Reincarnate: The Warning, The Maker, The Spaceman, The Realisation and The Reaper. The concept deals with the idea of a "musical soul" accompanying a human being through life and continuing through reincarnation after death. Wakeman presented it as a possibility rather than as an absolute explanation, exploring ideas about life, death, evolution and things that are difficult to explain. I found this particularly fascinating because of the spiritual dimension of the album. The recurring idea of the music of the soul, together with references to reincarnation and the journey of the soul, gives the music an additional meaning for me. The atmosphere is cosmic, epic, dramatic and almost cinematic, but also very beautiful and emotional.My favorite part is The Warning, especially its final section. There is a vocal passage that reminds me a lot of Jon Anderson, and when it becomes more dramatic, I absolutely love it. It is one of those moments that immediately caught my attention.The Maker has an incredible Rick Wakeman synthesizer passage that sounds unmistakably like him. It gives the album an enormous sense of grandeur and is one of the moments that most reminded me why I enjoy his work with Yes.I also really like The Spaceman, especially because of its beautiful melody and the way it continues the idea of the musical soul. The Realisation is another favorite. I love its melody and lyrics, and I found it particularly interesting how the album continues returning to the idea of the soul and its journey.The Reaper is also excellent. It has another wonderful melody and recalls ideas from earlier parts of the album, which gave me the impression of a return or continuation of the soul. This is my own interpretation, but I really enjoyed experiencing the album this way. The instrumental ending is also fantastic and reminded me of some moments from Yes.Finally, The Prisoner has a more dramatic character and fits very well into the overall atmosphere. The final piece, The Lost Cycle, also helps give the album a sense of completion, extending its ideas into questions about evolution and possible advanced civilizations beyond Earth. (Wikipedia)Honestly, I did not find any uninteresting moments here. For me, the album is beautiful from beginning to end.The vocals are also extremely important. They contribute greatly to the atmosphere and emotional impact of the album. Without them, I don't think No Earthly Connection would have the same character.The production is very good as well. Wakeman produced the album and played an impressive variety of keyboard instruments, including Moog synthesizers, Mellotron, Hammond C3 organ, pipe organ, grand piano, electric piano, clavinet and harpsichord. The instrumentation is very rich, but the keyboards and synthesizers remain the main identity of the record. (rwcc.com)At several points, the album reminds me of Yes, particularly because of Wakeman's keyboard style and the use of synthesizers. I can also hear similarities with other progressive rock bands from the 1970s.I wouldn't say that the album is radically original compared with everything else being produced in progressive rock at the time. I don't hear something that completely separates it from the progressive rock of its era. However, this does not take anything away from its beauty or magnitude.For me, the three greatest strengths are the vocals, the synthesizers and the melodies.I honestly cannot point to any significant weaknesses. The album works very well as a complete experience.Since this is the first Rick Wakeman solo album I have listened to, I cannot yet compare it with the rest of his solo discography. But this album certainly made me interested in exploring more of his solo work.I will definitely listen to No Earthly Connection many more times. It is an album that I enjoyed not only for its progressive rock qualities, but also because its ideas about the soul, reincarnation and existence gave the music a deeper personal meaning for me.Rating: 4/5No Earthly Connection is an album of beautiful melodies, impressive synthesizers, powerful vocals and grand progressive arrangements. Above all, for me, it is an album of music that feeds the soul.

items.body: Review by Prog Dog — I tend to root for the underdogs, and so The King of Limbs is the first Radiohead album I'm properly reviewing as I work my way through the catalogue. And, frankly, this one does have me puzzled.This is the album that seems to land near the bottom of the list for many Radiohead fans. It's their eighth studio album, and apparently it's the one you're supposed to approach with lowered expectations. Yet when I glance at the Wikipedia page, I find something rather different: The King of Limbs was named among the best albums of 2011 by a number of major music publications, and it went on to receive five Grammy nominations, including Best Alternative Music Album.So here I was thinking, Gosh, it must be too weird or weak? And it's a funny thing, too, that expectations can spoil a gift?or, depending on the circumstances, make it even better.But speaking frankly, I tend to like just about everything I hear from this band and its individual members. There's something about Radiohead that can always draws me in, and I think they set an example of artistic integrity that any band could and should learn from. "Wildness and mutations" were a couple of Thom Yorke's choice words describing it.The King of Limbs, it turns out, isn't overly grounded in the day-to-day. It's a subtle, glitchy, laid-back and pensive album. It unfolds like a pleasant daydream, scattered with illogical bits and flashes, hiding all sorts of secret messages and meanings. It's a trippy, sometimes ethereal, relaxing ride into an alternate timeline that Thom Yorke and friends have cooked up.The percussion?often looped?is peculiar throughout. The loops in a couple of the songs (1 and 4) remind me of riding the streetcars and subways of Toronto: that mesmerizing clickety-clack of the car rattling along while people and traffic carry on outside, the whole city moving around you as you gaze through the window.'Codex' was one of my favourites on the disc. It sits and fits so nicely among the rest of the songs. It's melancholic and soulful, with a slowly played, affected piano that moves along with a gentle kick drum, pumping like a heartbeat. Hard to believe they chose brass to adorn the song, but it works perfectly, thanks to the warmth and tenderness with which it's played and mixed. Then, near the end, the song briefly transforms, introducing an otherworldly orchestration paired with the most uncanny bloom of electronic noise?something that feels like invisible audio static cling.Moments like these are what make this album.Thom Yorke is a vocalist I find hard to quantify. I like his singing... a lot. Maybe I love it. He always sounds convincing, and somehow sells whatever it is he's meditating on. There's a fragility to his voice, too, and some kind of persona he embodies when he performs.Maybe that's it: he performs. He is really into it when he sings. He doesn't just deliver the melody or the lyrics; he channels something. There's a sense that he's inhabiting whatever emotional space the song occupies, rather than simply singing about it.For me, 'Little by Little' has that trademark stamp of a Radiohead composition: a simple, vanilla-flavoured guitar tone paired with low and mid notes ascending the guitar neck in that customarily wiggly way, teasing their way in and out of musical keys and defying logic to just the right degree. All the while, a crowded ensemble of various percussion instruments blip, shake and busily ticky-tick along. Refreshing!'Lotus Flower' feels like a jam, propelled by happiness-inducing handclaps. (I just can't imagine any other use for handclaps than to express joy.) I love how they use the most unsuspecting synthesizer tones to animate the chorus. They remind me of an old, weird plastic keyboard my cousins had in their basement back in the '70s, sitting next to their toy-like record player with records like 'Super Gold Hits' by K-Tel.My least favourite song melody-wise is 'Give Up the Ghost', but its lyrical sentiment redeems it somewhat for me. I've always liked the image it creates in my mind of coming home after a long day and turning to a spouse, a sibling, or a parent for an embrace when you're completely exhausted and ready to just give in.The final track is an appropriate send-off: 'Separator' is repetitive but starts to bloom and take off and soar a little after it's bleak beginning. "Wake me up, will you wake me up" No, Thom. We are enjoying the ride just fine, thank-you very much, and we should both just linger here a little longer... Prog dog album score: 4 bones out of 5.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — A couple of details set Starless and Bible Black apart from its contemporaries of the 1970s. The first was the departure of percussionist Jamie Muir, who left for a monastery after the recording of Larks' Tongues in Aspic, leaving Bill Bruford in charge of percussion. The second was the contribution of lyrics by Richard Palmer-James (Supertramp's original guitarist and a friend of John Wetton); he penned the words for "The Great Deceiver" and "Lament," which critique societal commercialism and fame, while "The Night Watch" serves as a study of the Rembrandt painting of the same name, and "The Mincer" appears to be a piece of free association. The album title, Starless and Bible Black, references a work by the poet Dylan Thomas. This speaks to the literary aspect, a significant source of inspiration that was very much in vogue at the time, though sadly, it has increasingly become a relic of that era today. Musically, the band, who had been improvising more and more during tours since the Islands era, incorporated several live improvisations into the album. What is remarkable is that, while these pieces clearly originated as improvisations, they are so well-structured that they possess a narrative arc, to use a literary metaphor, featuring an introduction, a climax, and a resolution. They offer a dramatic progression that tells a story: a composition with profound meaning that leaves the spirit fulfilled upon listening.A different concept infused the album, a different tempo: faster, more aggressive, and stripped of the lengthy preludes of the past. The bass and drum foundation was more prominent, and John Wetton stood out as both a great vocalist and a superb bassist. "The Great Deceiver" accelerates until the song suddenly begins to deconstruct, as if its parts were being dissected for minute analysis, a formula Fripp would further perfect in the future. And just like that...as abruptly as it begins, it ends...and "Lament" begins, full of calm and mystery.Wetton's voice is perfect for the kind of music Fripp was composing, music that was alive and evolving, changing from album to album; sometimes it would even change from concert to concert, without waiting for a recording to be made. David Cross's violin was the perfect companion... until the bass began to slice through the air, fracturing it, and Bruford, joined by Fripp, followed suit, corrupting and darkening the melody, just as Wetton's voice shifted to match the change, turning more aggressive. Then... the rhythm shifted once more, accelerating to a frenetic pace that the bass, drums, and guitar all tracked. Wetton's bass was funky and deeply groovy, while Bruford's drumming was all over the place, at times a cannonball, at others a machine gun, an entire arsenal at the service of the composition; he knew exactly when to hit the gas during the final coda and when to slam on the brakes, allowing silence to reclaim the stage, a true master of timing and its application."We'll Let You Know" is the first of those improvisations that are partly improvised yet don't quite seem like it; the opening, which never quite kicks into gear and seems to have no clear direction, actually reveals itself to be a perfectly crafted introduction for what follows. Once again, Wetton amazes with his unique feel and sensitivity, laying down a funk groove while Fripp sends musical streamers spiraling through the air... and when Bruford joins in, the whole thing explodes; without a doubt, Flea listened to this, alongside Funkadelic and Sly Stone, when composing the Red Hot Chili Peppers' Blood Sugar Sex Magik."The Night Watch", much like "Book of Saturday" was on the previous album, is the heart of Starless & Bible Black. With its Eastern atmosphere steeped in Japanese tradition (marking Fripp's first foray into that culture) and Wetton's sweet, relaxed, and wise vocals, the track achieves a magical "eclipse of the sun," driven by phrasing and Fripp's accompanying guitar work that have since become legendary. This is part of the band's magic, a quality that was never truly lost, as evidenced by "Matte Kudasai" in the 1980s lineup and "One Time" in the 1990s.During the recording of "Trio" at the Concertgebouw in Amsterdam, a piece driven entirely by Mellotron and violin, Bruford waited for the right moment to join in; however, deeming the performance perfect as it was, he never actually entered the song. The rest of the band considered this "lack of intervention" so precise, adding as much to the composition as if he had played, that it made him a composer of the piece "in his absence," just as much as they were through their actual participation.That tribal, and even almost playful air that The Mincer can possess vanishes as soon as the two concluding pieces (I'll call them "Suites") begin; they are improvisations akin to highways with a clearly marked, signposted route, and even when they ventured into dark jungles, the musicians knew where they were going and reached their destination, however much one might have doubted it at times. Starless and Bible Black begins gradually, so subtly, in fact, that one could say silence itself initiates it. Then, that guitar that sets everything ablaze emerges, like a distant alarm or a prehistoric wail. The Mellotron plays a pivotal role in crafting the album's universe; it is a descent into the underworld, where the bass and the impeccably precise drums only serve to heighten the tension. That Mellotron, paired with the bass, could almost pioneer a form of progressive funk, a fusion of the two genres unfolding beneath a musical landscape that is incredibly dense and complex."Fracture" is the album's other gem, the discovery that would serve as the cornerstone for the creation of Red. Fripp's counterpoints launch a highly distinctive opening melody; once revealed, it recedes, beginning a process of retreat and decomposition into its constituent parts. It is a symphony in which every member of the quartet has a role to play, both when they appear and when they vanish, like an act of sleight of hand. Bruford hints at what is to follow, albeit in a chamber-music style, before gradually building a "crescendo" worthy of high dramatic suspense. The momentum is occasionally slowed by the violin until the quartet suddenly surges forward in unison, fusing into a single entity; they stretch the main melody like modeling clay, molding it into various shapes and playing with it, yet never losing sight of the ultimate goal, even as parallel paths deliberately prolong the tension leading up to that final resolution. Wetton matches Fripp's intensity, with Cross and Bruford providing support as the pitch rises ever higher... until only the distorted guitar remains, left hesitating in the wake of the successfully executed "fracture." Everything was set for the next step, the final step, and the time for doubt was over.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There are many points where the style chosen by Mohini Dey touches upon the traditions of the 70s, both the virtuosity displayed on the bass, reminiscent of a great like Stanley Clarke, and that cosmic spirit that flowed not only through Return to Forever but also through the Mahavishnu Orchestra. That sort of jazz-style scat singing that opens "The Dey Way" is Konnakol, a form of vocal percussion from South India (also heard in Shakti with John McLaughlin); the 5-string slap bass gives it a punchy, defined sound, yet it isn't all sonic pyrotechnics, the music knows when to dial back the rhythm and calm the waters. What truly stands out is an abundance of hypnotic rhythm, complemented by Jonathan Mones's saxophone and bass lines that mimic the action of a sinuous defibrillator."Xtroverted Soul" features dissonant vocal harmonies that, in their ritualistic quality, truly recall the choral work of Zeuhl bands. Yet, it is a prime example of fusion at its best, with the guitar dancing in time to a perfectly integrated chorus that climbs ever higher in pitch, mirroring the saxophones. On "Whammy Award," one can hear keyboards as well as wind instruments, adding sonic variety, while her vocals are quite unconventional, reminiscent of Vinx, the soulful singer from Screaming Headless Torsos. And when she performs a bass solo, one can only conclude that Stanley Clarke's legacy is in good hands.The fusion with Indian rhythms makes the final result highly original, yet simultaneously recognizable and fresh, complemented by the spontaneity and joy she brings to her playing (much like Hiromi Uehara on the piano), which truly comes through in the music.When "Slappa Dey Bass" kicks in, the complexity of the arrangements clearly stems from the progressive nature of the compositions and the use of polyrhythms; as the trumpets and saxophones accelerate alongside the keyboards, the perfect atmosphere is created for her to improvise on the bass, displaying a style that quickly becomes familiar and establishes her own unique signature.With Joy, the band demonstrates its ability to craft a unique sound; the album feels gritty and street-smart yet sophisticated, simultaneously classic and modern. Echoes of Weather Report and Jaco Pastorius's style are audible, while "15 Steps Ahead" offers a more contemporary, electronic sound, featuring virtuosic performances of Eastern melodies and layered scales. At this point, the album engages in a nostalgic exercise, a nod to the past, as the chronological journey through history draws to a close, bringing us back to the postmodern present. Throughout, the playing remains organic and stirring."Uncle Dennis" is a highly syncopated funk track; with the horn section taking the lead, we hear the guest artist who gave the song its name: Dennis Chambers, a drummer known for his work with Mike Stern and Barbara Dennerlein, among others.The realm of possible sound is infinite; the final track, titled "Dad," pays homage to the very beginning of beginnings with a stripped-down, austere electric bass solo that speaks volumes.

items.body: The Prom on August 23, which was presented by the BBC Symphony Orchestra, conducted by Alain Altinoglu, concluded with a performance of Amérique by Edgard Varèses, having begun with Stravinsky’s Symphonies of Wind Instruments in its 1947 version, The Dvorak ‘Cello Concerto, with Gautier Capuçon soloist, and Debussy’s Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun. The title of the piece had dual meanings, just as Varèses’s intentions were multiple. The work was on one hand a sort of portrait of the active and bustling New York City, but it also had the intention of opening new, as it were, vistas of sound available for composition. The title implied both the new world as it existed, but also the possibility of exploration. So the music is full of energy and activity and the depiction of day to day noise in a specific way that was new in music. Although it has a momentary quite beginning (possibly referring to the beginning of The Afternoon of the Faun and offering a tribute to Debussy), Amérique’s energy and intensity is incessant and ever increasing. That intensity and energy was completely realized by this performance. The Prom on August 22 was presented by the Chineke! Orchestra, conducted by Jonathon Heyward and featured the soprano Angel Blue. It opened with a reconstruction of a work by the African American, British educated, at the Royal Academy of Music, composer, Edmund Thornton Jenkins. The work, which was conceived when he was a student in London, called Ballet, was reconstructed from existing parts and a piano reduction, by his great-newphew, Tuffus Zimbabwe. It was the first performance of any of Jenkins’s music on the Proms. The central work on the program was Samuel Barber’s Knoxville Summer of 1915, which featured Blue. The piece sets a text by James Agee and can be justifiably described as nostalgic. It is also arguably Barber’s best piece. The text is written in the first person, but Blue gave it a quality somewhat akin to what happens in Thorton Wilder plays, especially Our Town, where a character addresses the audience directly. She gave it an especially directly personal and expressive quality that was very moving and unforgettable. She followed the Barber with some songs from what is probably described these days as the American Song Book. Her performances of those pieces, including My Funny Valentine (Richard Rogers and Lorenz Hart), Our Love Is Here to Stay (Goerge and Ira Gershwin), That Old Black Magic (Harold Arlen and Johnny Mercer), and Puttin’ On the Ritz (Irving Berlin), was mostly masterful and compelling. For this listener the performance of My Funny Valentine compared favorably to Ella Fitzgerald’s recording. The order of the songs was not the same as what was listed in the program, and one of the songs listed was not performed. The concert concluded with a very lovely and lovely-sounding performance of the Dvorak Eighth Symphony. As is the current practice, the Prom on August 29, presented by the Oslo Philharmonic, conducted by Mirga Gražinytė-Tyla, was advertised as containing music by Stravinsky and Prokofiev without mentioning that it would be opened by the first Proms performance of Symphonic Poem no. 1, ‘Forest Morning’ by Øyvind Torvund. The work was as evocative as one might expect a piece with that title to be. It seemed to have at the beginning, random, or at least random seeming, recordings of birds, but those sound morphed into similar figures that were clearly played by instruments in the orchestra, so that after a while it wasn’t completely clear that there ever had been recordings of actual birds. The program quoted Torvund in saying “…I also like to think about all the smaller, perhaps psychedelic sounds in nature, those that are found naturally and can remind you of electronic sounds. The mirroring of sounds is one of the things that fascinates me the most.” So who knows? In any case, the shape and progress of the piece was compelling and impressive and very enjoyable. The Stravinsky work was the Violin Concerto, which was performed with the soloist Patricia Kopatchinskyaja. As her encore, regretting the absence of cadenzas and chances for soloistic displays in the piece, she played a very technically complicated and showy “candenza” which she had written based on material in the concerto. The concert concluded with a rousing performance of music from Romeo and Juliet by Prokofiev. As an encore at the end of the concert, the orchestra played another piece by Torvund, apparently orchestrated in the five previous days, entitled Starry Night. This one clearly made use of recorded sounds and was highly effective and also very enjoyable. The post BBC Proms Varese Barber Torvund Jenkins et al appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.body: Words by Justin TurfordThe Berlin-based Afro-fusion outfit Jembaa Groove have been on our radar since their debut album ‘Susuma’ brought their dreamy, light touch blend of soul and jazz-influenced highlife and Afrobeat to the world. Formed in late 2020 by Ghanaian percussionist, vocalist and songwriter Eric Owusu and Berlin born bassist, composer and producer Yannick Nolting (after a synchronous meeting whilst collecting their respective kids from kindergarten), Jembaa Groove was initially a 7-piece yet it has always been Eric and Yannick at the centre of the band and this new E.P. sees them working as a duo this time albeit with some very special guests in tow.Their musical backgrounds reveal much about where they are now. Eric was born in the Ghanaian capital, Accra but spent many years in Nigeria before developing into an accomplished sideman who regularly worked with highlife legends Ebo Taylor and Pat Thomas. Yannick’s peripatetic musical life has included jazz training in Germany before exploring traditional forms in various African countries, Brazil, India and Turkey as well as a number of years working with Lusophone artists in Lisbon. Add in a shared love of US soul and jazz and the richly coloured palette they work from is comparable to the UK Afrobeat-jazz septet Kokoroko, their laidback virtuosity similar but appreciably different. Yannick & Eric Their 2022 debut album ‘Susuma’ gained them immediate critical acclaim, smooth Afrobeat tracks like ‘Bassa Bassa’ showcasing their expert collage of Eric’s butter-rich multilingual vocals, jazzy chords, tight horn arrangements (check the Sir Duke-influenced horns on ‘Bassa Bassa’) and polyrhythmic groove sensibility. Not just anchored to Ebo Taylor style highlife, elements of Wassoulou music from Mali and Ghanaian (Akan people) Adowa became part of the band’s hybrid sound, a funky composite of influences that in their skilled hands feels remarkably natural. The second album ‘Ye Ankas / We Ourselves’ followed in 2024 and brought in guests K.O.G. and the great Gyedu-Blay Ambolley, the band stretching out in all directions but without losing what was now, an identity of their own.Onto 2026 and we have this four track E.P. ‘Be A Lover’, Yannick and Eric’s signature sound embellished by key guests from the UK, Nigeria and Mali. Having met the Nigerian highlife revivalist brothers The Cavemen at a festival in Amsterdam, Lagos came calling. In fact, Cavemen bassist Kingsley Okorie co-produced three of the tracks here and you can sense the pared-back space that The Cavemen have become synonymous with on these particular songs.The only song not involving the Nigerian brothers is the Yannick-produced opening number ‘No Pain No Gain’, which features East London-based but Nigerian-born, Ademola ‘Azekel’ Adesuyi. Viewed through an immigrant’s eyes, purposefully simple lyrics in English about resisting temptation and maintaining focus are sung beautifully over astral synths and glittering keys that Roy Ayers would surely love. Add sublime horns, a guitar motif by Nathan Badu that quietly embeds itself into your mind plus a rhythm section as relaxed and sensual as polyrhythmic percussion and bass can be and you have a perfectly judged Afrobeat-jazzy-R&B fusion deserving of a high chart position in a fair world. The brightly lit title track ‘Be A Lover’ sees The Cavemen’s Kingsley Okorie taking over bass duties as Lagos Afro-fusion artist Tim Lyre gives a heartfelt Afrobeats-esque vocal turn calling for love over violence - “be a lover, not a fighter”. The marriage of the classic 70s/80s percussion groove with polished guitar, synths and vocals (including harmonies from Eric and Kingsley) lends the song a delightful freshness, delivering quality Afro-pop without the omnipresent stain of autotune. The Cavemen: Benjamin James & Kingsley Okorie The Cavemen’s exuberant drummer and falsetto singer Benjamin James joins his brother Kingsley on the super-laidback ‘Obi’, probably the song most indebted to Ebo Taylor (or even the celebrated Igbo highlife legend Celestine Ukwu) on the record. Kingsley’s weary baritone intones softly over the most chilled of highlife grooves, his bass and his brother’s drums sitting back as dreamy electric guitars and languid horns take their sweet time. Benjamin’s wild falsetto interruptions bring a welcome friction to the otherwise elegant performance. The final song on this gorgeous record brings together a ‘supergroup’ of sorts. Jembaa’s Yannick and Eric and The Cavemen’s Benjamin and Kingsley are joined by one of the leading contemporary lights of Malian music, Fatoumata Diawara. Over (another) relaxed groove, the much-loved singer-songwriter and actress unveils her unmistakably powerful vocal in response to Eric’s quietly sung-spoken verses: a beautifully constructed contrast of human voices that is given another dimension from Benjamin as he throws out his own high-pitched exclamations.It’s great to see Jembaa Groove back and in such fine form. This E.P. feels like it just came together when the time was right, as unhurried as the tempo of the songs themselves. It’s also always a joy to discover new talents and I’ll be following Tim Lyre and Azekel from hereon. This is undoubtedly high quality Afro-fusion that can only build on their ever-growing global audience. 9/10.Released September 18th 2026.BUY HERE! https://jembaagroove.bandcamp.com/album/be-a-lover-ep

items.body: “I’d rather you feel something uncomfortable than nothing at all.” That is how BEEJAYBEE, a producer based in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, sums up his debut album. “VINAVVAVE” came out on 23 July 2026 as a self-released digital album on Bandcamp, and it also streams on Spotify. Across ten tracks the record mixes industrial timbre, analog noise and tape texture with a soul core and the pulse of Saigon’s house scene. VINAVVAVE by BEEJAYBEE The producer described the material in a message to Side-Line: “Just released my debut album, VINAVVAVE, ten tracks cut and reharmonized from raw analog texture, tape hiss, mechanical noise, the hum of machines that were never meant to be instruments. Physical sound pressure and industrial timbre wrapped around a soul core, carrying some of the pulse of Saigon’s own house scene, worked from the inside rather than sampled for effect.” The tracklist runs “NHO KHONG”, “MOI THI CHOI DUNG THI THOI”, “MAT CA TUOI”, “NHAN VUI”, “ANH BE LY CAY CHO”, “DAU DAU MUA”, “U NGON NGU NGANH”, “TU VIEN SAI GON”, “QUANG DAU” and “PHAI”. The album’s own notes describe it as moving in three stretches, opening dark and unrelenting. BEEJAYBEE’s home studio in Saigon The record was made almost entirely alone. BEEJAYBEE built a small home studio after arriving in Saigon and calls it his monastery. He described the road to it in the same message: “Built alone in a small home studio I call my monastery, after eighteen years inside China’s music industry […] then burning all of it down to start over here.” The name, the network and the earlier version of himself went with it; the album is, in his own words, a direct expression of the producer’s own body rather than a description of anywhere he has lived. About BEEJAYBEE BEEJAYBEE spent eighteen years as a producer inside China’s music industry before leaving that career and the name he had worked under. About two years before the album he moved alone to Ho Chi Minh City, where he set up a home studio and started again from a room, a machine and whatever sound was within reach. “VINAVVAVE”, self-released on 23 July 2026, is his debut album under the BEEJAYBEE name and the first result of that studio.

items.body: Sixteen tracks, most of them under three minutes, make up the first Scaled Alps album. The Los Angeles band released “Let the Alpine Play” on 20 July 2026 as a digital album on their own Blue Hell imprint, available on Bandcamp and on streaming services. Scaled Alps mix heavy rock, electronics and post-punk atmosphere under the low baritone voice of James Quentin Devine. Let the Alpine Play by Scaled Alps Devine sings, Anthony Percoco plays keys and guitars, Sean McCarthy plays drums and Steve Fishman plays upright and electric basses. Stewart Tuttle recorded the album at The Altar Studios in North Hollywood. The songs started as a set of self-recorded demos called “The Desertion Sessions”, cut in two sessions that ran through day and night and produced more than thirty tracks; sixteen of them were then re-recorded in the studio’s Big Room with Tuttle. On their Bandcamp page the band describe the result as “celestial, infernal crime spree music”. Devine described the project and the way the record was made in an email to Side-Line: “JQD is a low-voiced singer moving between heavy rock, electronics, post-punk atmosphere and stranger pop; the voice remains the stable identity while the machinery changes. The record itself was made rapidly and largely without a click, leaving breath, strain, drift and imperfections audible.” He points to “Southerly” and “Celestial Sighs” as starting points. ‘Let the Alpine Play’ tracklist The album runs “Another Clock Song (The 7th Unveiling)”, “Celestial Sighs”, “Southerly”, “Space/Time”, “Muffler (Chrome Viscera)”, “T.T.M.S. (Sunyata)”, “You Got H-O-R-S, You Want E Too?”, “Pink Diamonds”, “Neo Noir (Stelvio)”, “Selling It”, “Slow Motion”, “Impro (The Imp of the Perverse/The Pimp of the Inverse)”, “I Think We Met in Setagaya (Maybe it Was Seville)”, “Lemon Zest”, “Tentacoli” and “Throwaway Lines (Leo II)”. Only “Slow Motion” and “Lemon Zest” pass the three-minute mark; “Selling It” lasts 38 seconds. The band also publish an 18-page “Owner’s Manual” with the lyrics and the album’s visual material, and the full package of production WAVs and MP3s is offered as a free public download from the Blue Hell site. About Scaled Alps Scaled Alps is the band of Los Angeles singer and lyricist James Quentin Devine, who also records under his own name and as JQD, and of instrumentalist Anthony Percoco. The Scaled Alps name first appeared as a featured credit on Devine’s solo track “Cynical Ploy”, released on 5 May 2022, ahead of his solo releases “James Quentin Devine Plays the Saxophone For You” and “3-PIT” later that year. “Let the Alpine Play”, recorded at The Altar Studios in North Hollywood with Stewart Tuttle, Sean McCarthy and Steve Fishman, is the first full album under the Scaled Alps name and the first release on the band’s own Blue Hell imprint.

items.body: Musicians from Berlin, Pietrasanta and Ibagué make up Hellkern Warriors, and the gothic rock project’s fourth single, “Rain, Steam & Speed”, is out now as a self-released digital track on Bandcamp and the streaming platforms. The song runs 4:16 and came out on 18 April 2026. Hellkern Warriors mix analog synths, guitar, bass and drums with a cinematic production, and the lyrics deal with futurism, inner conflict and decay. Rain, Steam & Speed by Hellkern Warriors The band describes the track as “an urban nightscape of rain, neon lights, and unstoppable speed”. An official video accompanies the single, and the song currently tops the public vote in the Alternative category of the HOFA Song Contest 2026. Singer Tom Radar wrote to Side-Line that the new release “continues the sonic vision of our previous singles Petrol & Water and Helkern Warriors”. All three, plus “Endless Road”, are single tracks; the band has not released an EP or album so far. About Hellkern Warriors Hellkern Warriors formed in early 2025 as a four-piece spread across three countries. Drummer and producer Mauricio Castro (Ibagué, Colombia) initiated the project together with Alessandro Vezzoni (Pietrasanta, Italy), who plays synths under the names Kabal Apokalypse and Dylan Phoenix and runs Funeral Records Autoproduction; his earlier projects include Erotic Funeral, the EBM act Toxic Industry and the gothic rock project Binario 0. Tom Radar, singer and guitarist of the Berlin darkwave band Radarfield, took over lyrics, vocals and guitar after presenting the first demos in June 2025, and Colombian guitarist and bassist Fabian Parra, of Ghoulish Pain and Lemarchand, plays bass. Castro, who also drums in Impromtus ad Mortem and Lemarchand, mixes and produces the recordings at his own Artgot Studios. The band name refers to the Helkern computer worm. The debut single, spelled “Helkern Warriors” after the worm, appeared on 12 September 2025, followed by “Petrol & Water” on 1 November 2025 and “Endless Road” on 28 December 2025, both with official videos, and the band also appears on the compilation “Pulse In The Void – Vol.1”. “Rain, Steam & Speed”, out since 18 April 2026, is the fourth single, and the group collects the series under the working title “The Pulse of the Void”.

items.body: HANDS will return to Berlin’s Urban Spree on Saturday, 2 January 2027 for another New Year edition of HANDS Label Night, bringing together six live projects and two DJ sets for an evening moving through rhythm’n’noise, industrial techno and the harder edges of electronic music. The live line-up features SONAR, NULLVEKTOR, GREYHOUND, ICD-10, ESPECTRA NEGRA and MARIE, while HANDS founder Udo Wiessmann and HELLS will take care of the DJ sets. The night begins at 19:00, with doors also opening at 19:00. It is a particularly representative cross-section of the label’s history and current direction. SONAR, the Belgian project of Dirk Ivens and Eric Van Wonterghem, remain one of the defining names associated with rhythm’n’noise; their most recent HANDS album, “Future Cries”, arrived in 2023 after a nine-year album break. NULLVEKTOR, Stefan Böhm’s long-running project, connects industrial techno with rhythm’n’noise and has been part of the HANDS orbit since the early 2000s. GREYHOUND return with their uncompromising rhythmic approach, while ICD-10 arrive after releasing “Quantum Disruption” in May 2026, an album built around industrial-techno propulsion, seismic low-end pressure and tightly controlled rhythmic structures; it also includes a collaboration with GREYHOUND on “Merging Power”. ESPECTRA NEGRA, the project of Verónica Mota, brings the darker and more abrasive end of industrial techno to the bill, while MARIE completes the six-act live programme. The event also continues what has become a recurring Urban Spree tradition. HANDS staged its previous New Year Label Night there on 3 January 2026, following other Berlin editions at the same venue. The Dortmund-based label itself was founded by Udo Wiessmann in 1990 and became closely associated with the development of rhythm’n’noise while maintaining a catalogue extending into industrial techno, IDM, breakcore, ambient, electronica and sound art. HANDS Label Night Berlin – Saturday, 2 January 2027, Urban Spree Live: SONAR NULLVEKTOR GREYHOUND ICD-10 ESPECTRA NEGRA MARIE DJ: UDO WIESSMANN HELLS Doors / Start: 19:00 Both e-tickets and limited physical hard tickets are available through HANDS Bandcamp. For those who prefer to begin the year with considerably more noise than champagne, Berlin already has its first serious industrial appointment of 2027. About HANDS Udo Wiessmann founded HANDS in 1990 in his home town of Fürth in Franconia as an outlet for his own projects Atrum, Severance and Winterkälte, starting with limited-edition cassettes and industrial compilations. The first CDs followed in 1994 and the first vinyl, a Winterkälte 7″, in 1995. In the late 1990s the label moved to Dortmund and began issuing full albums on CD, opening with the debuts of Orphx, Ah Cama-Sotz and Needle Sharing and continuing with Mono No Aware, S.I.N.A. and Xabec. Winterkälte’s drum’n’noise records became reference points for the rhythm’n’noise scene, and the catalogue later extended into industrial techno, IDM, drum & bass, breakcore, ambient, electronica and sound art with acts including Nullvektor, Empusae, Geistform, Wieloryb, Monolith, Greyhound and Ontal, alongside reissues of The Klinik back catalogue. Between 1997 and around 2004 the label also ran the vinyl-only power electronics and noise sublabel 220N, and most of its sleeves and paper CD packs are designed by Nicola Bork. Live events sit at the centre of the label’s calendar. Wiessmann started the Forms of Hands label festival in 2001 with Michael Pfefferkorn and the promoter LaborNeun; since 2012 it has taken place at the Förderturm in Bönen in the Ruhr area, and each edition comes with a “Forms Of Hands” compilation of exclusive tracks by the acts on the bill. The Beats and Noise event at the Kulttempel in Oberhausen returns on 10 October 2026 with Sonar, Ancient Methods, Maschinenkrieger KR52, Hysteresis, ICD-10 and Mortaja. In Berlin, a HANDS Label Night at Bi Nuu marked the label’s 28th year in January 2018 before the series settled at Urban Spree, where it now runs twice a year: a summer edition (8 July 2023, 28 June 2025 and 27 June 2026) and a New Year edition. The sold-out 4 January 2025 night had Sonar, Eric De Vries, Greyhound, Templer, Espectra Negra and Phasenmensch on the bill, and 3 January 2026 brought Ah Cama-Sotz, Maschinenkrieger KR52, Supersimmetria, 16Pad Noise Terrorist and Incendie. The 2 January 2027 night is the third New Year edition of HANDS Label Night at Urban Spree in a row.

items.body: Ten singles into a twelve-single year, j:dead turns to the overthinking brain. The UK industrial project of Jay Taylor releases “Null” on 4 September 2026 via Infacted Recordings, the tenth entry in the monthly single campaign Taylor launched with “Pressure” in December 2025 and the follow-up to “Halo” of 7 August. Null by j:dead The lyric deals with a mind that will not switch off and keeps looking for something to feed it. Taylor described the starting point in his own words: “Null is about having an overactive, overthinking brain and the constant need to feed it with stimulation. For me, that can feel like both an escape from life and a coping mechanism. The song asks whether giving your brain the dopamine it constantly craves is a healthy way of coping, or simply another form of addiction.” Musically, “Null” mixes electro and industrial rock, pairing dark electronic production with the weight of a live band. Taylor said: “Sonically, this one continues to push me into new territory. It draws on electro and industrial rock, combining dark electronics and heavy rhythms with a more expansive, live-band-inspired sound.” The label’s own note on the release adds that heavy rhythms, driving electronics and industrial textures give the track “a scale designed to reach beyond the studio”. Taylor wrote, performed and recorded “Null” himself and shares the guitar parts with Hilger Tintel. Motel-Music produced the track, Studio-600 mastered it and Dokodemo created the artwork, the same team that worked on “Halo”. Where ‘Null’ sits in the j:dead single series The run started with “Pressure” on 5 December 2025 and has delivered one single a month since. “Disgusting” followed, then “Who Knows”, “Feeling Alone”, “Silence Calls” and “Over The Years”. “Keep Walking” arrived on 5 June 2026 as the seventh single, “Draws My Blood” on 3 July as the eighth, and “Halo” on 7 August as the ninth. “Null” is number ten, which leaves two more singles to close the twelve-month cycle. About j:dead j:dead is the solo project of Jay Taylor, based in Bicester, England. Before starting the project in late 2019, Taylor drummed live for Tactical Sekt, Tyske Ludder and Harmjoy. The first j:dead singles, “Haunt” in 2019 and “Feeding On Me” in 2020, led to the debut album “A Complicated Genocide”, issued by the German label Infacted Recordings in January 2021 on CD and digital. The single “Tearing Me Apart”, featuring Teknovore, and “I’ll Wait” followed the same year. 2022 brought a cover of “DAS OM3N”, the four-track EP “Vision of Time” on Infacted Recordings, the single “Hold Tight” and two collaborations, “High Time (Chinese Takeaway)” with FabrikC and “Thrive” with Nature Of Wires. In 2023 Taylor released “Surrendering”, a cover of “You Spin Me Round (Like a Record)” with Menschdefekt, the single “Harbour” and the EP “ROOTS”, and “What We’ll Be” appeared in 2024. The monthly single campaign that began with “Pressure” in December 2025 now reaches its tenth release with “Null”.

items.body: Thirteen new extended versions, cut from the original tapes, make up the next Telex release. “MAXI” arrives on Mute on 4 December 2026 as a double album on transparent red and blue vinyl and as a CD, with a digital release to follow in 2027. The launch track is a maxi version of “Moskow Diskow”, the 1979 single from the Belgian synthpop trio’s debut album, now out as official audio on Mute’s YouTube channel. The album is available to pre-order. Telex were Marc Moulin (1942-2008), Dan Lacksman and Michel Moers, and the two surviving members went back to the original tapes to build the Maxi versions, which come with new mixes and new mastering. The album collects “Moskow Diskow”, “Soul Waves”, “L’Amour Toujours”, “Rock Around The Clock”, “Temporary Chicken”, “Dance To The Music”, “Eurovision”, “En Route Vers De Nouvelles Aventures”, “Rendez-Vous Dans L’Espace”, “Peanuts”, “Twist À Saint-Tropez”, “Spike Jones” and “We Are All Getting Old”, each carrying the “(Maxi)” suffix. The tracklist spells the opener “Moskow Diskow”, as on the original single, while the audio upload titles it “Moscow Diskow”. Telex revisit ‘Euro-vision’ and ‘Rock Around The Clock’ Two of the extended tracks come with a television history. “Euro-vision” was Belgium’s entry at the Eurovision Song Contest in 1980, where it finished 17th of 19 with 14 points. Moers described the entry as “very Situationist International, the worm in the apple.” The band set out to finish either first or last, and did neither. Their cover of Bill Haley’s “Rock Around The Clock”, slowed down and sung through a vocoder, brought the trio an invitation to perform on Top of the Pops in 1979; Mute calls it “a ticking, vocoderised, supremely deadpan robot parody of the original”. The later material on “MAXI” includes the cut-up “rap” of “Peanuts”, from 1988’s “Looney Tunes”, and “Rendez-Vous Dans L’Espace”. About Telex Telex formed in Brussels in 1978, when Marc Moulin, Dan Lacksman and Michel Moers set out to make electronic pop without guitars. Their first single was a cover of Les Chats Sauvages’ “Twist à Saint-Tropez”, and the debut album “Looking for Saint-Tropez” (1979) carried “Moskow Diskow” and “Rock Around The Clock”. “Neurovision” followed in 1980, the year of the Eurovision entry, and “Sex” in 1981, with lyrics co-written with Sparks. “Wonderful World” appeared in 1984 and “Looney Tunes” in 1988, after which the trio remixed its catalogue as “Les Rythmes Automatiques” in 1989 and then went quiet as a recording unit. The sixth and last studio album, “How Do You Dance?”, came out in 2006. Moulin died on 26 September 2008, and Telex announced their retirement that year. The partnership with Mute began in 2021 with “This Is Telex”, a 14-track compilation released on 30 April 2021 with the tracks newly mixed and remastered by Lacksman and Moers. It added two previously unreleased covers, “Dear Prudence” by The Beatles and “The Beat Goes On” by Sonny & Cher, both found while the compilation was being assembled. Mute then reissued the six studio albums, remastered from the original tapes, as a limited vinyl and CD “Telex” box set, announced in October 2022 with the teaser “EP1” and released on 14 April 2023. Three days later Lacksman and Moers sat down with Mute founder Daniel Miller for a public talk in Brussels (A night with Telex and Mute Records founder Daniel Miller in Brussels). Moers went on to release his second solo album, “As Is”, in 2024, led by the single “Microwaves” with Claudia Brücken of Propaganda. “MAXI” is the first Telex release of newly made versions since that box set, and the third stage of the Mute campaign after the compilation and the reissues.
